title: Beyond the Sky and the Earth
author: Jamie Zeppa
blurb: A young Canadian teacher’s first impressions of Bhutan’s overwhelming landscape, written with wonder and poetic language.
source: Zeppa writes about her arrival in Bhutan as a young teacher from Canada
heading: From Beyond the Sky and the Earth: A Journey into Bhutan - Jamie Zeppa
context: When Zeppa was 24 years old she left Canada to teach in Bhutan. This memoir grew out of an essay she wrote about her early days in the country.

paragraphs.html: Mountains all around, climbing up to peaks, rolling into valleys, again and again. Bhutan is all and only mountains. I know the technical explanation for the landscape, landmass meeting landmass, the Indian subcontinent colliding into Asia thirty or forty million years ago, but I cannot imagine it. It is easier to picture a giant child gathering earth in great armfuls, piling up rock, pinching mud into ridges and sharp peaks, knuckling out little valleys and gorges, poking holes for water to fall through.

It is my first night in Thimphu, the capital, a ninety-minute drive from the airport in Paro. It took five different flights over four days to get here, from Toronto to Montreal to Amsterdam to New Delhi to Calcutta to Paro. I am exhausted, but I cannot sleep.

From my simple, pine-paneled room at the Druk Sherig hotel, I watch mountains rise to meet the moon. I used to wonder what was on the other side of mountains, how the landscape resolved itself beyond the immediate wall in front of you. Flying in from the baked-brown plains of India this morning, I found out: on the other side of mountains are mountains, more mountains and mountains again. The entire earth below us was a convulsion of crests and gorges and wind-sharpened pinnacles. Just past Everest, I caught a glimpse of the Tibetan plateau, the edge of a frozen desert 4,500 meters above sea level. Thimphu's altitude is about half of that, but even here, the winter air is thin and dry and very cold.

The next morning, I share breakfast of instant coffee, powdered milk, plasticky white bread and flavorless red jam in the hotel with two other Canadians who have signed on to teach in Bhutan for two years. Lorna has golden brown hair, freckles and a no-nonsense, home-on-the-farm demeanor that is frequently shattered by her ringing laughter and stories of the wild characters that populate her life in Saskatchewan. Sasha from British Columbia is slight and dark, with an impish smile. After breakfast, we have a brief meeting with Gordon, the field director of the WUSC program in Bhutan, and then walk along the main road of Thimphu. Both Lorna and Sasha have traveled extensively; Lorna trekked all over Europe and northern Africa and Sasha worked for a year in an orphanage in Bombay. They are both ecstatic about Bhutan so far, and I stay close to them, hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm.

Although Thimphu's official population is 20,000, it seems even smaller. It doesn't even have traffic lights. Blue-suited policemen stationed at two intersections along the main street direct the occasional truck or landcruiser using incomprehensible but graceful hand gestures. The buildings all have the same pitched roofs, trefoil windows, and heavy beams painted with lotus flowers, jewels and clouds. One-storied shops with wooden-shuttered windows open onto the street. They seem to be selling the same things: onions, rice, tea, milk powder, dried fish, plastic buckets and metal plates, quilts and packages of stale, soft cookies from India−Bourbon Biscuits, Coconut Crunchies and the hideously colored Orange Cream Biscuits. There are more signs of the outside world than I had expected: teenagers in acid washed jeans, Willie Nelson's greatest hits after the news in English on the Bhutan Broadcasting Service, a Rambo poster in a bar. Overall, these signs of cultural infiltration are few, but they are startling against the Bhutanese-ness of everything else.

The town itself looks very old, with cracked sidewalks and faded paintwork, but Gordon told us that it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago. Before the sixties, when the third king decided to make it the capital, it was nothing but rice paddies, a few farmhouses, and a dzong−one of the fortresses that are scattered throughout the country. Thimphu is actually new. "Thimphu will look like New York to you when you come back after a year in the east," he said.

At the end of the main road is Tashichho Dzong, the seat of the Royal Government of Bhutan, a grand, whitewashed, red-roofed, golden-tipped fortress, built in the traditional way, without blueprints or nails. Beyond, hamlets are connected by footpaths, and terraced fields, barren now, climb steadily from the river and merge into forest. Thimphu will never look like New York to me, I think.

The Bhutanese are a very handsome people, "the best built race of men I ever saw," wrote emissary George Bogle on his way to Tibet in 1774, and I find I agree. Of medium height and sturdily built, they have beautiful aristocratic faces with dark, almond-shaped eyes, high cheekbones and gentle smiles. Both men and women wear their black hair short. The women wear a kira, a brightly striped, ankle-length dress and the men a gho, a knee-length robe that resembles a kimono, except that the top part is exceptionally voluminous. The Bhutanese of Nepali origin tend to be taller, with sharper features and darker complexions. They too wear the gho and kira. People look at us curiously, but they do not seem surprised at our presence. Although we see few other foreigners in town, we know they are here. Gordon said something this morning about Thimphu's small but friendly "ex-pat" community.

When we stop to ask for directions at a hotel, the young man behind the counter walks with us to the street, pointing out the way, explaining politely in impeccable English. I search for the right word to describe the people, for the quality that impresses me most−dignity, unselfconsciousness, good humor, grace−but can find no single word to hold all of my impressions.

In Thimphu, we attend a week-long orientation session with twelve other Irish, British, Australian and New Zealand teachers new to Bhutan. Our first lessons, in Bhutanese history, are the most interesting. Historical records show that waves of Tibetan immigrants settled in Bhutan sometime before the tenth century, but the area is thought to have been inhabited long before that. In the eighth century, the Indian saint Padmasambhava brought Buddhism to the area, where it absorbed many elements of Bon, the indigenous shamanist religion. The new religion took hold but was not a unifying force. The area remained a collection of isolated valleys, each ruled by its own king. When the Tibetan lama Ngawang Namgyel arrived in 1616, he set about unifying the valleys under one central authority and gave the country the name Druk Yul, meaning Land of the Thunder Dragon. Earlier names for Bhutan are just as beautiful−the Tibetans knew the country as the Southern Land of Medicinal Herbs and the South Sandalwood Country. Districts within Bhutan were even more felicitously-named: Rainbow District of Desires, Lotus Grove of the Gods, Blooming Valley of Luxuriant Fruits, the Land of Longing and Silver Pines. Bhutan, the name by which the country became known to the outside world, is thought to be derived from Bhotanta, meaning the "end of Tibet" or from the Sanskrit Bhu-uttan, meaning "highlands".

While the rest of Asia was being overrun by Europeans of varying hue but similar cry, only a handful of Westerners found their way into Bhutan. Two Portuguese Jesuits came to call in 1627, and six British missions paid brief but cordial visits from the late 1700s until the middle of the next century. Relations with the British took a nasty turn during the disastrous visit of Ashley Eden in 1864. Eden, who had gone to sort out the small problem of Bhutanese raids on British territory, had his back slapped, his hair pulled, and his face rubbed with wet dough, and was then forced to sign an outrageous treaty that led to a brief war between the British and the Bhutanese. Considering the consolidated British empire in the south, and the Great Game being played out in the north between the colonial powers, Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable. I am full of admiration for this small country that has managed to look after itself so well.

bhutan-only.quote: Bhutan is all and only mountains
bhutan-only.what: Emphatic statement using 'all and only' for absolute effect.
bhutan-only.effect: Immediately establishes Bhutan's defining characteristic - overwhelming mountainous terrain.

cannot-imagine.what: Admits geological explanation beyond her comprehension.
cannot-imagine.effect: Shows humility and human perspective versus scientific facts.

giant-child.quote: giant child gathering earth in great armfuls, piling up rock, pinching mud into ridges and sharp peaks, knuckling out little valleys and gorges, poking holes for water to fall through
giant-child.what: Series of playful verbs - 'pinching', 'knuckling', 'poking' - creates child playing with clay.
giant-child.effect: Makes incomprehensible geology accessible through imaginative, tactile imagery. Whimsical tone.

five-flights.quote: five different flights over four days
five-flights.what: Specific details emphasise difficulty reaching Bhutan.
five-flights.effect: Establishes Bhutan's isolation - not easy to reach even by modern transport.

exhausted-cannot.quote: I am exhausted, but I cannot sleep
exhausted-cannot.what: Physical exhaustion overcome by mental stimulation.
exhausted-cannot.effect: Shows the overwhelming nature of the experience - too much to process.

simple-pine.what: Alliterative 'pine-paneled' suggests basic but natural materials.
simple-pine.effect: Establishes unpretentious setting - focus on natural not luxurious.

mountains-moon.quote: mountains rise to meet the moon
mountains-moon.what: Mountains actively 'rise to meet' - given agency.
mountains-moon.effect: Creates romantic, mystical atmosphere. Mountains seem alive.

baked-brown.what: Alliterative description emphasises heat and dryness of India.
baked-brown.effect: Sharp contrast with cool, mountainous Bhutan.

mountains-more.quote: on the other side of mountains are mountains, more mountains and mountains again
mountains-more.what: Repetition of 'mountains' creates sense of infinity.
mountains-more.effect: Conveys overwhelming scale - mountains never end.

convulsion.quote: convulsion of crests and gorges and wind-sharpened pinnacles
convulsion.effect: Mountains seem actively tormented, not peacefully settled.

tibetan-plateau.quote: Tibetan plateau, the edge of a frozen desert 4,500 meters above sea level
tibetan-plateau.what: Specific altitude gives scale Western readers can grasp.
tibetan-plateau.effect: Provides concrete measurement to understand extreme altitude.

thin-dry-cold.quote: thin and dry and very cold
thin-dry-cold.what: Three adjectives build harsh environmental picture.
thin-dry-cold.effect: Emphasises physical challenge of the environment.

instant-coffee.quote: instant coffee, powdered milk, plasticky white bread and flavorless red jam
instant-coffee.what: Adjectives emphasise artificial, processed nature of food.
instant-coffee.effect: Shows isolation from fresh ingredients - everything preserved/imported.

no-nonsense.what: Compound adjectives capture Canadian prairie personality.
no-nonsense.effect: Quick character establishment through cultural stereotypes.

ringing-laughter.effect: Makes Lorna seem vibrant and alive despite harsh setting.

slight-dark.quote: slight and dark, with an impish smile
slight-dark.effect: Creates contrast with sturdy, practical Lorna.

ecstatic.what: Strong emotional word shows their excitement.

stay-close.quote: I stay close to them, hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm
stay-close.what: Physical proximity sought for emotional support.
stay-close.effect: Shows narrator's insecurity and need for reassurance.

no-traffic.quote: It doesn't even have traffic lights
no-traffic.what: 'Even' emphasises this as basic urban infrastructure.
no-traffic.effect: Establishes Thimphu as barely urban by Western standards.

incomprehensible-graceful.effect: Shows cultural gap but with admiration not frustration.

stale-soft.effect: Shows disadvantages of isolation - old imported goods.

acid-washed.effect: Dated Western fashion seems incongruous in Bhutan.

willie-nelson.what: Specific American artist in Buddhist kingdom.
willie-nelson.effect: Absurd juxtaposition of Texas country and Himalayan kingdom.

rambo-poster.quote: a Rambo poster in a bar
rambo-poster.what: American violent action hero in peaceful Buddhist nation.

startling.what: Shows narrator's surprise at Western infiltration.
startling.effect: These elements don't belong - jar against setting.

bhutanese-ness.what: Creates new word to capture unique quality.
bhutanese-ness.effect: Suggests something indefinable but recognisable about Bhutan.

cracked-faded.effect: Sets up surprise that it's actually new.

didnt-exist.quote: it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago

nothing-but.quote: nothing but rice paddies, a few farmhouses, and a dzong
nothing-but.what: 'Nothing but' emphasises how little was there.
nothing-but.effect: Shows dramatic transformation from rural to urban.

look-like-ny.quote: Thimphu will look like New York to you when you come back after a year in the east
look-like-ny.effect: Warns that Thimphu is modern compared to rural Bhutan.

grand-whitewashed.effect: Creates sense of majesty and traditional beauty.

without-blueprints.effect: Shows sophisticated engineering without modern tools.

never-look.quote: Thimphu will never look like New York to me, I think
never-look.effect: Shows narrator's enchantment with Thimphu's uniqueness.

best-built.quote: the best built race of men I ever saw
best-built.what: 18th century colonial language about physical appearance.
best-built.effect: Shows consistent Western admiration across centuries.

i-agree.what: Confirms historical observation with personal experience.
i-agree.effect: Links past and present Western perspectives.

beautiful-aristocratic.quote: beautiful aristocratic faces with dark, almond-shaped eyes, high cheekbones and gentle smiles
beautiful-aristocratic.what: Multiple beauty markers create idealised portrait.

kira.quote: kira, a brightly striped, ankle-length dress
kira.what: Explains foreign garment for Western readers.

gho.quote: gho, a knee-length robe that resembles a kimono
gho.what: Uses familiar Asian garment to explain unfamiliar one.
gho.effect: Makes foreign concept accessible through comparison.

look-curiously.quote: look at us curiously, but they do not seem surprised
look-curiously.what: Notes being object of curiosity without hostility.
look-curiously.effect: Shows Bhutanese politeness and previous exposure to foreigners.

ex-pat.what: Quotes marks suggest ambivalence about term.

dignity-grace.what: List of qualities shows struggle to capture essence.
dignity-grace.effect: Shows complexity of impression beyond simple description.

no-single-word.quote: no single word to hold all of my impressions
no-single-word.what: Admits language fails to capture experience.
no-single-word.effect: Suggests something transcendent about Bhutanese character.

most-interesting.what: Superlative shows genuine engagement with history.
most-interesting.effect: Shows narrator becoming invested in understanding Bhutan.

druk-yul.quote: Druk Yul, meaning Land of the Thunder Dragon
druk-yul.what: Provides English translation of Dzongkha name.
druk-yul.effect: Makes country seem mythical and powerful.

just-as-beautiful.effect: Narrator falling in love with country through its names.

southern-land.effect: Shows Bhutan valued for natural resources and beauty.

south-sandalwood.effect: Makes country seem exotic and valuable.

rainbow-district.quote: Rainbow District of Desires, Lotus Grove of the Gods, Blooming Valley of Luxuriant Fruits, the Land of Longing and Silver Pines
rainbow-district.what: Series of increasingly fantastical place names.
rainbow-district.effect: Makes Bhutan seem like earthly paradise or fairy tale.

overrun-europeans.quote: overrun by Europeans of varying hue but similar cry
overrun-europeans.what: 'Varying hue but similar cry' - different nations, same imperialism.

nasty-turn.what: Colloquial phrase marks shift to conflict.

back-slapped.quote: back slapped, his hair pulled, and his face rubbed with wet dough
back-slapped.effect: Makes diplomatic insult visceral and memorable.

preservation-remarkable.quote: Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable
preservation-remarkable.effect: Shows Bhutan's exceptional status in Asia.

full-admiration.quote: I am full of admiration for this small country that has managed to look after itself so well
full-admiration.what: Personal emotional response to historical facts.
full-admiration.effect: Ends with genuine respect for Bhutan's achievement.

demeanor.note: American spelling of demeanour - how someone conducts themselves.
demeanor.effect: Helps establish Lorna's practical, straightforward character.

trefoil.note: Architectural term for decorative three-part design common in Buddhist architecture.
trefoil.effect: Shows traditional Bhutanese architectural style with Buddhist symbolism.

shamanist.note: Religion based on shamans who communicate with spirit world.
shamanist.effect: Shows Buddhism merged with existing spiritual practices.

felicitously.meaning: In a pleasing or apt manner
felicitously.note: Perfectly chosen or expressed - particularly appropriate.
felicitously.effect: Emphasises how beautifully named Bhutanese places are.

overview.heading: Why Zeppa Wrote This
overview.intro: Zeppa's purposes evolve through the passage:

points.label: To capture first impressions
points.text: "It is my first night in Thimphu" - Documents initial experience

points.label: To educate about Bhutan
points.text: "without blueprints or nails" - Shares cultural knowledge

points.label: To celebrate independence
points.text: "Bhutan's preservation of its independence was remarkable" - Admires resilience

points.label: Those interested in cultural preservation
points.text: References to "ex-pat community" and Western infiltration

points.label: Anxious newcomer
points.text: "hoping to pick up some of their enthusiasm" - Uncertain, seeking confidence

points.label: Appreciative learner
points.text: "I am full of admiration" - Respectful and impressed

points.label: Poetic descriptor
points.text: "just as beautiful" - Enchanted by language and names

points.label: Childlike imagery
points.text: "giant child gathering earth" - Makes geology magical

points.label: Sensory description
points.text: "plasticky white bread", "stale, soft cookies" - Tactile disappointment

points.label: Poetic names
points.text: "Rainbow District of Desires" - Enchanting place names

points.label: Juxtaposition
points.text: "Willie Nelson" vs "lotus flowers" - Old meets new

points.label: Opening with landscape
points.text: "Bhutan is all and only mountains" - Establishes setting

points.label: Personal to historical
points.text: Moves from personal experience to historical context

points.label: Paradox revealed
points.text: "it didn't exist thirty-odd years ago" - Ancient-looking is new

points.label: Ending with admiration
points.text: "I am full of admiration" - Concludes with respect
